title: Overview
heading: Overview
text: Open-source application portfolio management Know every application, and what to do with it AppWren is one living record of every application an organization runs: who answers for it, what it is for, what it is built on, what it costs, and how healthy it is. From that record it works out a recommendation for each one, and shows the reasoning. Get started Try the demo Source on GitHub

title: Overview
heading: The reasoning is on the screen
text: Every score opens to its factors, levels, weights, and sources, and every recommendation to the rule that produced it. Nothing is typed in as a verdict.

title: Overview
heading: People decide
text: The system recommends. A named person records what will be done and why. Where the two differ, both are shown, and neither overwrites the other.

title: Overview
heading: Unknown is not zero
text: A fact nobody has recorded is left out of the score and counted against confidence. Too little known means Assess , never a guess.

title: Overview
heading: Quiet by design
text: No scanners, collectors, or agents, and no access to anything else on the network. It records what people know and decide. Scores

title: Overview
heading: Four scores, each with its working
text: Business value, technical health, cost and burden, and risk exposure are worked out from the record and from what assessors answered. Each opens to the factors behind it, the level each stands at, its weight, and where the fact came from. Beside them is data confidence: how much of each score's weight is known, and which missing facts would raise it most, each with a link to where it is entered. How a score is worked out Recommendations

title: Overview
heading: A recommendation, and the rule behind it
text: Invest, maintain, tolerate, modernize, replace, consolidate, retire, incubate, or assess: rules are tried in order, and the record names the one that matched. A guardrail protects what must not go without a successor. A Retire for the only provider of a capability, or for a system of record for regulated information, becomes Replace , and the working says why. Recommendations Decisions

title: Overview
heading: A decision is a person's, with a reason and a date
text: Whoever leads the unit, or the portfolio team, records the disposition: what will be done, why, by when, and when to look again. The scores as they stood that day are kept with it. A decision that differs from the recommendation is not an error. It is listed as a mismatch with its reason, so a review starts from the cases worth talking about. Decisions and mismatches Overlap

title: Overview
heading: What are we paying for twice?
text: Applications are mapped to the capabilities they serve. Every capability served by more than one is listed with those applications side by side: scores, recommendation, decision, how many people use each, and what each costs. Name a primary provider, and the others that are worth less are recommended for consolidation. Overlap Impact

title: Overview
heading: What breaks if this goes?
text: Before a retirement is recommended, an application's Connections say what it would touch: what depends on it, directly and in turn, the interfaces that would stop, and the capabilities left with nothing behind them. It also says which units use it, up to how many people, and what its record says must outlive it, such as active studies or data that must be kept. What breaks if this goes Data flows

title: Overview
heading: Follow a class of data from system to system
text: An interface records data passing from one application to another: by what method, how often, and which classes of data it carries. Choose a class to see every interface that carries it and every application that holds it. Where an interface delivers a class the receiving application's record does not list, the flow is marked, because that application's risk is understated until someone settles it. Follow a class of data Lifecycle

title: Overview
heading: What falls out of support, and what runs on it
text: Components are built on technology releases, and each release has a day its support ends. The timeline shows the releases in use, soonest first, with how many components in how many applications are on each. Support dates can be typed, or brought in from a file of end-of-life data that you supply. An application on a release past its date scores worse for it, and one that also holds restricted data is flagged. Lifecycle Cost

title: Overview
heading: What it costs, line by line, and who pays
text: An application's cost is a list of lines: a license, hosting, a support contract, your own people's time, each with what pays for it. A grant has an end date, and an application paid for by one that ends within a year is flagged until someone decides what becomes of it. Contracts carry their renewal and notice dates and whether a data agreement is in place. Cost and contracts are shown only to those who may see them, and a total is given whole or not at all. Cost and contracts Capabilities

title: Overview
heading: The capability map, measured
text: The map shows what the organization does, and how many applications stand behind each part of it: none, one, or an overlap. Measure it by any score, by data confidence, or by the health of the weakest application behind each capability, since a capability is as exposed as the worst thing it rests on. The capability map, measured Connections

title: Overview
heading: What is this connected to?
text: Every record opens to a picture of what it is joined to: what it depends on, where its data goes, the capabilities it serves, what it is built on, where it runs, and the contracts and funding behind it. A list beside the picture says the same in full, and all of it works from the keyboard. Records the reader may not see are counted, never named. How a record is connected Data handling

title: Overview
heading: Which applications hold health data, and how well are they kept?
text: Choose a class of data and get the applications that handle it, with what an analysis of risk asks about each: who answers for it, where it runs, how people sign in, the support state of what it is built on, and whether a data agreement is in place. The same rows export as a spreadsheet. Who handles a class of data Keeping current

title: Overview
heading: A record that says when nobody has looked at it
text: The people who keep an application confirm its record in one step, every six months for the most critical and every year for the rest. They are reminded before it falls due and after; if it stays late, their steward hears, then their leader. A record past its date says so on its page, in data quality, and in its scores: its data confidence is fifteen points lower until someone confirms it, so a portfolio that goes stale cannot look as sure of itself as one that is kept. Confirm the record Campaigns

title: Overview
heading: Ask the owners, and see who has answered
text: A campaign asks everyone who answers for the applications in a unit to confirm their records, or to assess them, by a date. Before it starts it says whom it would ask, and which applications have nobody to ask. There is nothing to tick: an application is done when its record is confirmed or it is assessed. The campaign's page shows coverage by unit, least covered first, each figure the length of the list behind it. Campaigns Tasks

title: Overview
heading: What happens raises a task for whoever must act
text: A contract's notice date near, a release in use nearing the end of its support, a grant ending, an owner leaving: each raises a task for the person who must act, with a date and the reason. A cause raises one task, never two, and the task closes by itself when its cause is settled. When someone leaves, everything they held is listed, and passed on in one step. Tasks Planning change

title: Overview
heading: From a decision to a change that is done
text: A portfolio review draws its agenda from what needs deciding in a unit, and keeps what it decided. A decision to change something becomes an initiative with its applications and dates, on a roadmap, in one step. A request for something new is shown what already serves the need before anything is bought. An application cannot move on without what its next stage requires, and a retirement is a checklist that ends with its savings on record. Planning change Facts from other systems

title: Overview
heading: Facts that arrive by themselves, and never over a person
text: Connectors an administrator switches on, one at a time, read what other tools already know: support dates from the public end-of-life dataset, what each repository says about its component, and who signs in to what. Your own tools post the rest with a key that can do nothing else. Each value is marked with where it came from and when, is in the history like any change, and can be overridden by whoever keeps the record, with a reason. Nothing is connected until someone connects it. Facts from other systems Engineering maturity

title: Overview
heading: Bronze, silver, or gold, from checks rather than claims
text: Monitoring, backups, and documentation from the record; tests, continuous integration, dependency updates, and open alerts from the repository. Each component reaches the level its checks give, and its application the level of its least mature part, with what is missing for the next. By unit, each count is a link to the list behind it. Where a source supplies them, these signals join the scores, and an application without one scores as before. Engineering maturity The program

title: Overview
heading: See what a change would do before you make it
text: The lists, the organization's own fields, the wording of the questions, and the scoring model's weights, thresholds, and cadence are shaped in the app. A changed model is previewed first: every application whose scores, recommendation, or flags would move is listed. Publishing makes a new version and changes exactly those; every decision keeps the scores it saw. Shape the program Home

title: Overview
heading: One page of what each person owes
text: Most people who keep an application are not portfolio specialists. Home lists what is theirs to do: an application to assess, a record to confirm, a task, what a campaign asks, a record that lacks what its stage requires. A bell counts what is new, and email is there if you want it. The dashboard gives the portfolio team the whole: recommendations beside decisions, flags, confidence, and what everything costs, with every figure a link to the list it counts. Home and the dashboard

title: Overview
heading: One definition of an application
text: Applications, their components, and where each runs are separate records, so the portfolio compares like with like.

title: Overview
heading: Judged by the right rubric
text: A shared platform is judged on what rests on it, and research software on whether it can be kept going. A pilot is not judged on use at all.

title: Overview
heading: Ready for research
text: Grant funding and its end dates, studies that depend on an application, research data classes, and software kept by one person are all part of the record.

title: Overview
heading: Working on the first day
text: The vocabularies, a starter capability map of 43 capabilities, a question bank, and a scoring model with its profiles, rules, and flags come with a new installation.

title: Overview
heading: A program you can change
text: The questions, weights, thresholds, and rules are yours to change. Each version is kept, and every assessment and snapshot names the one it used.

title: Overview
heading: A history that holds
text: Every change is in an append-only, hash-chained log, with who made it. An auditor reads everything and changes nothing.

title: Overview
heading: The portfolio as it stood
text: A snapshot keeps every application's scores, recommendation, and decision on a day, so a review can be compared with the one before. One is kept each month by itself.

title: Overview
heading: Find anything
text: One search across every kind of record, from the command palette. Any list's filters are kept under a name, and shared if you wish.

title: Overview
heading: Say a score is wrong
text: An owner contests a factor with the evidence; the portfolio team accepts or answers it, and both stay on the record.

title: Overview
heading: Written down once
text: Adding an application whose name, alias, or product is close to one on record shows that one first.

title: Overview
heading: In and out
text: Applications come in from a spreadsheet, with a dry run that reports every problem by row. Every list exports as CSV, and as JSON through the API.

title: Overview
heading: Who sees what
text: Roles are held over units. Sensitive fields, costs, and contracts are withheld from those who may not see them, in every list, figure, and export.

title: Overview
heading: Where it runs
text: Hosting platforms list everything on them by environment: what would stop if a data center or a cloud account were lost.

title: Overview
heading: Sign in your way
text: Local accounts out of the box. Optional single sign-on by OpenID Connect, built to work with Microsoft Entra ID, with roles and units taken from the provider.

title: Overview
heading: Open and yours
text: Apache 2.0 with no paid edition. SQLite on a laptop or PostgreSQL on a server, no build step, and your own name and colors.

title: Overview
heading: Try it

Clone the repository and build the demo organization: a fictional research institute with a clinic, two years of history, 107 applications, three survey tools doing one job, a grant about to end, a database release reaching the end of its support, and a decision that differs from its recommendation. git clone https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/appwren.git cd appwren uv sync uv run appwren demo uv run appwren --config demo/appwren.toml serve Open http://127.0.0.1:8020 . The sign-in page offers eight sample people and asks for no password. Start as the portfolio manager. Explore the demo organization says who to try next, and Getting started sets

title: Overview
heading: Where it stands
text: These pages describe version 0.8.0: the portfolio, the landscape around it, and the means of keeping both current. It signs in with local accounts or, if you set it up, single sign-on, and sends email only if you ask it to. Every fact is still typed or imported by a person: read-only connectors to the tools that already know them come next, then review cycles, initiatives, and the retirement playbook. The roadmap says what comes next and in what order, and the changelog lists what is in each release.

title: Adopting AppWren
heading: Adopting AppWren
text: Adopting AppWren This guide is for an organization deciding whether to take up AppWren, and for whoever will lead it there. It says what AppWren asks of you, what to settle before installing anything, and a path from nothing to a running program in about a quarter.

title: Adopting AppWren
heading: Is it for you?
text: AppWren suits an organization that wants to know what applications it runs, who answers for each, and what to do with them, and wants the answers kept true by the people who know them rather than by a central team chasing. It is built for a few hundred to a few thousand applications; the measurements go to five thousand. It is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. It runs on one server, on SQLite for a small team or PostgreSQL for many people at once, and reaches out to nothing an administrator has not switched on. It is not an asset database for every server and laptop, a ticketing system, or a project tracker. It holds applications and the parts of them worth deciding about, and links

title: Adopting AppWren
heading: Try it first
text: The demo organization shows every screen with two years of history, and needs nothing set up: uv run appwren demo uv run appwren --config demo/appwren.toml serve Sign in as any of its sample people from the sign-in page. Spend an hour as the portfolio manager, then as an application owner: the second view is the one that decides whether a program will last. See Explore the demo organization .

title: Adopting AppWren
heading: Before you install anything
text: Settle Because Who owns the program One named person, usually in IT strategy, enterprise architecture, or the CIO's office, who will hold the quarterly reviews and make the leadership reports What the units are Every application belongs to a unit. Take them from the organization chart, two or three levels deep, not deeper Who decides Managers decide anywhere; leaders decide for their units. Nobody decides about an application they answer for Where it will run A server you look after, a container platform, or a virtual machine; PostgreSQL if more than a few dozen people will use it at once. See Deploy How people will sign in Single sign-on with your identity provider is better than passwords:

title: Adopting AppWren
heading: Weeks 1 and 2: stand it up
text: Install it ( Getting started ), or start the container recipe . Begin from the starter program closest to your organization. Connect single sign-on and email, and make it look like yours: your name, logo, colors, and, if you say department where AppWren says unit , your words ( Appearance ). Add the units and the portfolio team. Give a second person the administrator role. Run uv run appwren doctor --production and fix what it says. Set up appwren backup to run every night, and restore one backup somewhere else once, to know it works ( Back up and restore ).

title: Adopting AppWren
heading: Weeks 2 to 4: make the program yours
text: Read Shape the program , then change only what you are sure of: the definition's examples in your organization's words, the tiers' descriptions, the domains, and the fields you will really fill in. Leave the scoring model as it is until you have seen it score your own applications; every factor and weight is described in the engine , and a change is previewed before it is published.

title: Adopting AppWren
heading: Weeks 4 to 6: a pilot with one or two units
text: Import their applications, name an accountable owner for each, and run a confirmation campaign. Sit with two or three owners while they confirm and assess, and change what confuses them. A pilot that ends with every record confirmed and assessed, and one portfolio review held, is ready to widen.

title: Adopting AppWren
heading: Weeks 6 to 12: open the door
text: Import the rest, a few units at a time, each with its own campaign. Turn on the connectors your organization can use ( Facts from other systems ), so that support dates, code activity, and sign-ins arrive without anyone typing them. Hold the first review in each unit that has finished its campaign. At the end of the first quarter, make a leadership report . From then on, the program handbook describes the rhythm.

title: Adopting AppWren
heading: Connecting other systems
text: Reading the portfolio: issue an API token for the system that needs it, with the least role that will do and for reading only. Being told when something happens: register a webhook for decisions, stage changes, and lapses. Facts your own tools know: a push key lets a script post incidents, tickets, and the like onto records ( Facts from other systems ).

title: Adopting AppWren
heading: What has been checked, and what has not
text: AppWren's code has been reviewed against the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard, level 1, and every screen is checked for accessibility on each release; the record is in the review . The review was of the code, not a penetration test of a deployed installation, and no person has yet used it with a screen reader. An organization with its own security or accessibility team should have them look before relying on it for anything sensitive.

title: Adopting AppWren
heading: What AppWren will not do
text: It will not decide for you. It recommends, with its working shown; a named person decides, and the decision is kept. It will not count what nobody can open. Every figure is the length of a list someone may see. It will not send anything anywhere you have not set up: no telemetry, no calls home. It will not change its history. Every change is kept, hash-chained, and can be verified with appwren verify .

title: Getting started
heading: Getting started
text: Getting started This guide takes you from nothing to a running AppWren that your organization can sign in to. It is for whoever installs it and sets it up. Allow about fifteen minutes. If you only want to look around first, skip to Explore the demo organization .

title: Getting started
heading: What you need
text: uv , which provides the right Python (3.12 or later). A copy of this repository. Every command in these guides is run through uv run appwren … from the repository directory. The full list is in the command reference .

title: Getting started
heading: Install
text: uv sync

title: Getting started
heading: Set up the installation
text: uv run appwren init init does six things: Writes appwren.toml , the deployment settings, in the current directory. Creates the data home, ./var , which holds everything that is not in the database. Creates the database. With no other setting, this is a SQLite file inside the data home. Asks for your organization's name, and a first unit within it if you wish, such as your team. Every application belongs to a unit, so this is the least you need to add one. Press Enter to skip it and add units later. Loads the default program: the vocabularies (lifecycle stages, sourcing, tiers, data classes, interface methods, environments, cost categories, and the rest), what each lifecycle stage requires of

title: Getting started
heading: Start from a program shaped like yours
text: The default program suits a research organization with some clinical work. If yours is another kind, begin from a starter program instead: the default program as that kind of organization would first change it, with its own capability map, domains, kinds of unit, data classes, funding, and examples of what counts as an application. The question bank, the scoring model, and the lifecycle are the default's, so every application is assessed and scored the same way. Starter For starter-research-institute An independent research institute: labs and core facilities, grant-funded software, research data starter-academic-medical-center Hospitals and clinics beside research and teaching, a fuller cli

title: Getting started
heading: Check it
text: uv run appwren doctor doctor checks the configuration, the data home, that the database answers, that its schema is the one this version expects, that the database still refuses changes to the history, and that the history verifies. It exits with 1 if anything must be fixed.

title: Getting started
heading: Run it
text: uv run appwren serve The server prints its address, by default http://127.0.0.1:8000 . Use --port to pick another port. serve refuses to start in three cases, and says what to do in each: It says Do this The database schema is behind uv run appwren db upgrade There is no administrator yet uv run appwren users add you@example.org --name "Your Name" --role admin The port is already in use Stop what is using it, or pass --port As installed, AppWren listens only on the machine it runs on. To put it in front of other people, read Configuration first.

title: Getting started
heading: Sign in for the first time
text: Open the address in a browser and sign in with the email address and password you gave init . AppWren signs in with local accounts: an email address and a password that it keeps. Nothing else has to be installed or connected. Signing in with your organization's identity provider, such as Microsoft Entra ID, is optional and can be added at any time: see Single sign-on . Five failed attempts within fifteen minutes stop sign-in for that account from that address for a few minutes. A sign-in ends after 12 hours without activity, and after 7 days in any case. Both are settings . To change your password, open the account menu at the top right and choose Your account . Changing it signs out your ot

title: Getting started
heading: Set up the organization
text: The administrator account sets the installation up. It does not keep applications or record decisions: that belongs to the roles below, and an administrator who also does that work is given a second role.

title: Getting started
heading: Units
text: Admin → Units holds the organization as a hierarchy of any depth: divisions, departments, centers, core facilities, labs, clinics, offices, and teams. Every application belongs to a unit, roles can be limited to a unit and everything beneath it, and figures roll up the tree. Give each unit a short code; imports refer to units by it.

title: Getting started
heading: People and roles
text: Admin → People adds accounts and gives them roles. A person with no role is a member: they can read the catalog, and they keep the applications they are named on. Role What it is for Manager The portfolio team. Edits any application, records decisions, takes snapshots, and shapes the program. Can be limited to a unit Architect Keeps the records the whole organization shares (capabilities, technologies, vendors, hosting platforms, and funding sources) and assesses applications. Can be limited to a unit Leader Leads a unit. Sees it and everything beneath it, and records decisions for its applications Steward Keeps a unit's applications complete and current: adds, edits, imports, and assesses t

title: Getting started
heading: Import units and people
text: Both screens take a CSV file, which is the quick way to load an organization. Each import can be run dry first and reports every problem by row, so nothing is half-loaded. The import dialog shows the columns it expects.

title: Getting started
heading: Appearance
text: Admin → Appearance sets the product's name, your organization's name, a logo, an accent color, and the default palette. See Running the program .

title: Getting started
heading: Start with one team
text: AppWren does not need the whole organization to begin. A single team that keeps a few dozen applications can use it for its own, and the rest of the organization can join later without anything being redone. Make the organization the top unit, and the team a unit within it. init asks for both (or pass --organization and --first-unit ). The organization is only a name until others join. If you began with the team at the top, Admin → Units → Put a unit above the top adds the organization above it later, with everything beneath the team moving with it. Add the departments that use your applications as units with nobody in them, so that each application can say who uses it, and the dashboard and

title: Getting started
heading: Bring in your applications
text: Most organizations start from a spreadsheet. Applications → Import reads a CSV file, matches its columns to AppWren's fields, and runs dry first, reporting every problem by row. A row with a reference already on record updates that application; any other row adds one. See Import and export . Then give the stewards of each unit a week to fill the gaps. Reports → Data quality shows, unit by unit, what is missing.

title: Getting started
heading: Explore the demo organization

title: The portfolio
heading: The portfolio
text: The portfolio This guide is for everyone who keeps, assesses, or reads the record of an application: the people named on applications, the stewards of units, architects, leaders, and the portfolio team. It covers what an application is, the record and what each stage of its life requires, components and what they are built on, capabilities, assessment, the scores and the working behind them, recommendations, flags, decisions, cost and contracts, and import and export. What joins applications to one another is in The landscape .

title: The portfolio
heading: What counts as an application
text: An application is software, or a service built from software, that people name, use for a purpose, and could decide to keep, change, or retire as one thing. An application Not an application The grants management system A server or a database on its own: record it as a component of what it serves The learning management system A report or a module of a larger system: a component of that system A lab's sample tracker, used by three labs A spreadsheet one person keeps for themselves The research data warehouse A programming language or a platform: a technology Holding to one definition is what lets the portfolio compare like with like. The definition is part of the program, and the form for a

title: The portfolio
heading: The record
text: Portfolio → Applications lists every application you may see, with its scores, its recommendation, and the decision on record. Filter it by lifecycle stage, sourcing, tier, domain, or unit; search by name or reference; and choose Mine for those you are named on. Each application has a permanent reference, such as APP-0042 , that never changes or is reused. Its page has nine parts: Part What it holds Overview The scores, the recommendation and the decision, the people named on it, what its record still needs, and every field Scores Each dimension's working, the rule behind the recommendation, and what would raise confidence Assessment The latest answers, who gave them and when, and every asse

title: The portfolio
heading: The fields
text: Besides its name, its summary, and its unit, an application's fields come in sections: Section Fields What it is Lifecycle stage and since when; sourcing (SaaS, Commercial run here, Built here, Open source run here, Low-code, Research software, or Vendor-hosted custom); purpose (Mission, Operations, Insight, Foundation); pace (Steady, Evolving, Experimental); domain; criticality tier, from 1 (mission critical) to 5 (minimal); other names it goes by Where it comes from Vendor, product, edition or version, hosting, its address, and its documentation Who uses it About how many people use it, and whether people outside the organization do Who supports it How many people can maintain it, and the

title: The portfolio
heading: People named on it
text: Every application has exactly one accountable owner , the person who answers for it. Whoever adds an application is accountable for it until they hand it on. Others may be named as business owner, technical owner, product manager, support contact, data steward, security contact, or executive sponsor, and as many of each as it needs. Anyone named on an application may change who else is named. Only the accountable owner, the steward of its unit, or an architect or manager whose scope includes it may hand on the accountability. An application whose accountable owner has left is flagged No accountable owner and listed on its steward's home page.

title: The portfolio
heading: What each stage requires
text: An application moves through eight lifecycle stages: Proposed, Evaluating, Phase-in, Active, Containment, Phase-out, Retired, and Archived. Each stage asks more of the record than the one before, and the record says what is still missing, now and before the next stage: Stage Requires, in addition to the stages before Proposed A summary, its sourcing, and the capabilities it serves Evaluating An accountable owner, its purpose, and its data classes Phase-in Its tier, hosting, supporting unit, annual cost, and funding Active How people sign in, monitoring, backup, users, maintainers, domain, pace, what its components are built on, and a current assessment Containment A decision about what to do

title: The portfolio
heading: Links and other systems
text: An application can be recorded as depending on another, as part of another, or as replacing another. Data passing between two applications is recorded as an interface . How many active applications depend on one, by a link or by receiving its data, is part of its business value. It can also carry its references in other systems: a configuration item, a ticket queue, a repository, its sign-in registration, a contract number, or a governance record. Search finds an application by any of them, and each is shown as a link where the program gives its system an address pattern .

title: The portfolio
heading: Restricted applications
text: An application can be marked restricted , which hides even its existence from everyone except the people named on it, the stewards and leaders of its unit, architects and managers whose scope includes it, auditors, and administrators. Use it sparingly: a portfolio is useful in proportion to how many people can find what already exists.

title: The portfolio
heading: Components and what they are built on
text: Portfolio → Components lists the parts of applications: services, web front ends, databases, batch jobs, integrations, reports, modules, libraries, mobile apps, analysis pipelines, and infrastructure. A component belongs to one application and takes its unit and its visibility from it. Each component records the technologies it is built on, and which release of each. That is what makes technology currency a fact rather than an opinion: AppWren knows when each release reaches end of support. Landscape → Technologies holds the languages, frameworks, runtimes, databases, operating systems, platforms, and products the organization uses, each with its releases and their support dates, its vendor,

title: The portfolio
heading: Capabilities
text: A capability is something the organization does, such as Biospecimen tracking or Participant surveys , named for what it does, not for the software that does it. Landscape → Capabilities shows the capability map: the default program's 43 capabilities in five areas (Research, Clinical care, Education, Administration, and Information technology), each with how many applications serve it. An application's Capabilities part says which it serves. Where several serve one, one of them can be named its primary provider. This is how AppWren finds overlap: an application that serves a capability whose primary is another, is primary for none, and is worth less than that primary, is recommended for Cons

title: The portfolio
heading: Assessment
text: An assessment is a set of answers to the question bank, given by a named person on a date. The questions are kept for judgment; anything that can be measured is a field instead. Dimension Questions Business value How closely does it support what the organization is trying to achieve? How well does it do what its users need today? Will the organization still need what it does in three years? Technical health How well does it meet the service its users expect? How easy is it to change, upgrade, and keep current? How confident are we in the vendor and the product's future? (asked only of vendor-sourced applications) Cost and burden How much effort does it take to keep running? How much effort d

title: The portfolio
heading: The scores
text: Every application in service has four scores, each from 1 to 5, where 5 is always best for the organization : Score Asks 5 means Business value How much would the organization lose without it? A great deal Technical health How well is it built, run, and kept current? Very well Cost and burden What does it take to keep? Little Risk exposure What could go wrong while it is kept? Little Each score is the weighted average of its factors . A factor comes from an answer ( strategic fit ), from a field ( criticality from the tier, security from the sign-in method), from a number in bands ( reach : fewer than 10 users is 1, at least 1,000 is 5), or from a calculation over the record ( technology cur

title: The portfolio
heading: Unknown is not zero
text: A factor with no data is left out of its score, never assumed. The score is worked out from what is known, and coverage says how much of the score's weight that was. A score with less than half its weight known is thin : it is shown, with its coverage, and it cannot carry a recommendation. Data confidence is the average coverage of the four scores. Below 70%, the recommendation is Assess . Beside it, AppWren lists what would raise confidence : each unknown factor, the heaviest first, with a link to where it is entered. A factor can also be not applicable : vendor viability for software built here, or technology currency for a SaaS product. It is left out of the score and of the weight confid

title: The portfolio
heading: The working
text: Choose any score to see how it was worked out: each factor, its level, its weight, and why it has that level ( Answered in the assessment ; 380 people: bands 10, 50, 250, 1,000 ; The only active application for Biospecimen management ), with any factor that is unknown or not applicable and the reason, and the sum. The Scores part shows the same for all four at once, with the assessment the answers came from and who gave it. Every figure can be redone by hand from what the screen shows. A value a connector or a push source supplied names its source, and the signals other tools supply, such as incidents or dependency alerts, count only where a source supplies them: see Facts from other systems

title: The portfolio
heading: Profiles
text: Not every application is judged by the same rubric. The scoring model has three profiles , and the first that matches applies: Profile Applies to What differs Foundation Shared platforms (purpose Foundation) Judged on what rests on them: reach and dependents weigh more Research software Sourcing Research software Judged on whether it can be kept going: sustainability and maintainability weigh more Standard Everything else Some facts also set a floor : an application that active studies depend on, or that is a system of record for regulated information, has business value of at least 4.0. The working names the floor and why.

title: The portfolio
heading: Recommendations
text: The scores, the lifecycle stage, and the record together give a recommended disposition . Rules are tried in order, and the first that matches gives the recommendation; the Scores part names it. Disposition When it is recommended What it means Incubate Proposed, Evaluating, or Phase-in; or experimental and under a year old New; not yet judged on use Assess Confidence under 70%, or value or health thin Not enough is known to say Consolidate It does what a capability's primary provider does, and is worth less Move its users to the primary Invest Value and health at least 3.0, and cost and burden at least 3.0 Grow its capability and use Maintain Value and health at least 3.0, but costly to keep

title: The portfolio
heading: The portfolio chart
text: Portfolio → Portfolio chart places every scored application by business value against technical health, or against cost and burden. Each bubble is sized by its cost, where you may see costs, and colored by risk exposure. The threshold lines divide it into the quarters the rules use. Hover over a bubble to see which application it is and where it stands, and click it to open the application. A table beneath gives the exact figures for every application on the chart, and the applications too little is known about to place are listed after it.

title: The portfolio
heading: Flags
text: Flags are raised whatever the recommendation. Each is a separate signal, with its own words, and names the facts that raised it. Flag When Restricted data on unsupported technology It holds restricted data, and something it runs on is past end of support No accountable owner Nobody answers for it Grant ending It is paid for by a grant that ends within a year, and nobody has decided what to do with it this year One person keeps this Built here, low-code, or research software, tier 1 to 3, with one maintainer or none Assessment expired Its latest assessment is no longer current Decision review due The decision on record is past its review date Archive before retiring It is to be retired, repla

title: The portfolio
heading: Decisions
text: The engine recommends; a person decides. A decision records a disposition for an application by a named person, with a rationale, a date to review it (a year on, unless you choose another), and, if you wish, a target date. A decision to consolidate names the application its users will move to. Managers record decisions for any application, and leaders for the applications of their units. Nobody records a decision about an application they are accountable for, unless the program lets owners decide (see Shape it in the app ); then each decision a manager or leader records about their own application is marked Recorded by its own owner . To record one, open the application and choose Record a d

title: The portfolio
heading: Mismatches
text: When today's recommendation differs from the decision on record, the application shows a mismatch : both dispositions side by side, each with its working. A mismatch changes nothing on its own; it is a prompt for the next portfolio review. Portfolio → Decisions lists them, beside the decisions whose review date has come and the applications nobody has decided about yet.

title: The portfolio
heading: What it costs
text: An application's Cost part says what it costs a year, and how much that is for each person who uses it. The figure can be typed on the record as a rough estimate, or broken down into cost lines : A line says What it is for A license or subscription, hosting, a support contract, your own people's time, or something else How much a year What pays for it A funding source : an operating budget, a grant, a chargeback, a capital project The contract it falls under Optional. Naming one makes that contract cover the application Choose Break it down , or Edit the lines , to change them. Once an application has lines, its annual cost is their sum , and the figure on the record can no longer be typed o

title: The portfolio
heading: Funding sources
text: Funding sources are kept by architects and managers, under Portfolio → Contracts → Funding sources . Each has a kind, a code such as a cost center or grant number, and, for a grant or a project, the day the money stops. Its page lists what it pays for.

title: The portfolio
heading: Contracts
text: Portfolio → Contracts holds the agreements with vendors that applications run under: Vendor, number, start, and end The end is the end of the current term Notice, in days How long before the end the vendor must be told, if it is not to renew. The list shows the date this makes, and marks it when it is within 90 days or has passed Renews by itself Whether it renews unless someone says otherwise Yearly value and licenses bought Data agreement Whether an agreement covers the data the vendor handles: in place, not needed, or missing What it covers The applications, and how many of the licenses each uses Narrow the list to contracts ending within 90 days, six months, or a year. Stewards, architec

title: The portfolio
heading: Import applications
text: Applications → Import reads a CSV file: Choose the file. AppWren reads its header and guesses which column is which field; correct any guess, or leave a column out. Run it dry. Every problem is reported by row and column, and nothing is saved. Import. All the rows are saved, or none of them. A row whose reference is already on record updates that application, through the same checks as an edit by hand. Any other row adds one. The accountable owner is given by email address, and the vendor by name. A row that names nobody accountable is imported, and its application is flagged No accountable owner . A value for a sensitive field you may not see is refused. Stewards, architects, and managers i

title: The portfolio
heading: Export
text: Every list can be exported as CSV from its Export button: applications, components, interfaces, deployments, contracts, funding sources, vendors, technologies, hosting platforms, capabilities, the applications that handle a class of data, and, from a list that a dashboard figure opens, the portfolio with its scores, recommendations, and decisions. The same exports come as JSON through the API . An export holds only what you may see, with the filters you have chosen. Values that a spreadsheet would treat as a formula are prefixed so that they are shown as text, and each export is recorded in the history.

title: The portfolio
heading: Next
text: To see the whole portfolio's figures and what is missing from its records, read Running the program . To connect another system, read the API guide .

title: The landscape
heading: The landscape
text: The landscape This guide is for architects, the portfolio team, and anyone who needs to see an application in its surroundings: what it exchanges with others and what data passes, what depends on it, where it runs, what else does the same job, and what it is built on that is falling out of support. The portfolio covers one application's record; this guide covers what joins them.

title: The landscape
heading: Interfaces
text: An interface is data passing from one application to another. It is a record of its own, with a reference such as INT-0015 , and says: From and To The application the data comes from, and the one it goes to. Two different applications Method An API call, a file transfer, a scheduled extract and load, a shared database, messages or events, an embedded page, or by hand How often As it happens, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, or when someone asks Data it carries The classes of data that pass, from the same list an application's record uses Owner Who to ask about it To record one, open either application, choose Connections , and then It sends data or It receives data . The people who keep eithe

title: The landscape
heading: A consumer depends on its source
text: An application that receives data depends on the one that sends it, just as a recorded depends on link says. Both count, once each, toward the source's dependents , which is part of its business value. Recording what a system feeds can therefore raise its score, and its working says how many depend on it.

title: The landscape
heading: Follow a class of data
text: Landscape → Data flows shows where each class of data travels. Choose a class to see every interface that carries it and every application that holds it. Where an interface delivers a class that the receiving application's record does not list, the flow is marked. Either the interface carries less than was recorded, or the application's record needs the class added. AppWren cannot know which, and changes neither; but until somebody does, that application's risk exposure is understated, because it is worked out from the classes its record lists.

title: The landscape
heading: How a record is connected
text: Every application, component, capability, technology, vendor, interface, hosting platform, contract, and funding source has a picture of what it is joined to. Open it with How it is connected on the record, or The picture on an application's Connections. The record is in the middle, with its neighbors in groups: what it depends on and what depends on it, where its data goes and comes from, the capabilities it serves, its components, what they are built on, its vendor, where it runs, and the contracts and funding behind it. The + on a neighbor shows what lies beyond it. Choosing a neighbor puts it in the middle. Tab moves through the records; Enter on a record puts it in the middle, and on it

title: The landscape
heading: What breaks if this goes
text: An application's Connections part begins with what would be touched if it stopped: what depends on it directly, and what depends on those in turn; the interfaces that would stop; the capabilities left with no application at all, and those that would lose their primary provider; the units that use it, and up to how many people use it or anything that depends on it (the same person may use several, so this is an upper bound); what its record says must outlive it: that active studies depend on it, that it is a system of record, that its data must be kept. Read it before recommending a retirement. A Retire for the only provider of a capability is already turned into Replace by the engine; this p

title: The landscape
heading: Where it runs
text: Landscape → Hosting holds the hosting platforms things run on: data centers, cloud accounts, compute clusters, hosting providers, a vendor's own service, or people's own computers. Architects and managers keep them, each with its kind, its provider, and where it is. A deployment says that an application, or one of its components, runs in an environment (production, staging, test, development, or disaster recovery) on a platform, optionally at an address. To record one, open the application, choose Components , then Say where it runs . Leave the name empty and it is named for what runs and where: Tracker API, production . A platform's page lists everything on it, by environment: what would st

title: The landscape
heading: Overlap
text: Landscape → Overlap lists every capability served by more than one application in service, with those applications side by side: their four scores, the recommendation, the decision on record, how many people use each, and what each costs where you may see it. The primary provider is named first. An application that serves a capability whose primary is another, and is worth less, is recommended for Consolidate . Where no primary is named, none of them is recommended for consolidation: name one on its Capabilities part. As a list opens the same applications in the portfolio list, where they can be exported. A total of cost is shown only when you may see the cost of every application in it.

title: The landscape
heading: The capability map, measured
text: Landscape → Capabilities shows the map. Above it, choose what to measure each capability by: Measure Shows How many serve it The number of applications in service: none, one, or an overlap Business value, Technical health, Cost and burden, Risk exposure The average over the applications that serve it Weakest health The technical health of the weakest application that serves it: a capability is as exposed as the worst thing it rests on Data confidence How much is known about the applications that serve it Each figure is a number with the score's own bar, and opens the applications it was worked out from. A broader capability is measured over every application beneath it, each counted once.

title: The landscape
heading: Lifecycle
text: Landscape → Lifecycle shows the technology releases applications run on, soonest end of support first. Each is a bar from the release's first day to the end of its support, with today marked, and beside it the state, the date, and how many components in how many applications are on it. Narrow it to what is past its end of support, ending within a year, or supported. Every release on record adds the releases nothing runs on. Applications with a planned retirement are listed beneath. The counts here are the same as on each technology's page, which names the applications.

title: The landscape
heading: Which applications run on a release
text: To answer "which applications run on .NET 6?", open the technology and, beside the release, choose As a list . The applications list opens narrowed to it, and Export gives the same rows as a spreadsheet. Every application on it does the same for every release, and the card of components that name no release has its own list. An application is on a release when any of its components is. The same narrowing works in the address and through the API: technology (a reference), with release (a release's cycle, or none ), or version (an exact version as recorded, such as 6.0.25 , or its start, such as 6.0 ). The components list takes them too. Each list is cut to what the reader may see, like any ot

title: The landscape
heading: Radar
text: Radar , reached from Technologies or Lifecycle, shows the technologies in use by the organization's view of each for new work: Adopt , Trial , Assess , or Hold , each with its kind and how many components run on it. Technologies that are in use and that nobody has placed are listed apart: someone should say whether new work may use them. An application all of whose technologies are supported scores better for technology currency if every one is Adopt , and worse if any is on Hold .

title: The landscape
heading: Support dates from a file
text: Support dates can be typed on each technology's page, brought in from a file, or read by the end-of-life connector once an administrator switches it on, so that nobody types them. For a file, AppWren fetches nothing: you bring it. On each technology, set its End-of-life key : the name the file knows it by, such as python or postgresql . Get a JSON file of end-of-life data. text: Reports → Data handling lists the applications in service that handle a chosen class of data, with what an analysis of risk asks about each: Column What it says Application Its tier, unit, and sourcing Accountable Who answers for it, or that nobody does Where it runs Its platforms in production, or its hosting, and its vendor Sign-in How people sign in to it Built on The worst support state among what its components run on, and the releases Carries it How many interfaces carry the class into it and out of it Data agreement Whether a contract that covers it has one in place, needs none, or lacks one Export gives the same rows as a spreadsheet. title: Keeping current
heading: Keeping current
text: Keeping current This guide is for everyone who keeps an application, and for the portfolio team. It covers how AppWren keeps the record true without a central team chasing it: what is waiting on you and how you are told, confirming a record, campaigns, the tasks that what happens raises, passing on what someone holds, finding anything, and saying a score is wrong.

title: Keeping current
heading: What is waiting on you
text: Home lists what is yours to do, most urgent first: an application not assessed or whose assessment has expired, a record due to be confirmed, a task, what a campaign asks of you, a flag on one of your applications, what a record lacks for its stage, and a portfolio review you run that is coming up. The bell in the top bar counts what is new for you. It opens Notices : each reminder, task, campaign, and answer, newest first, with a link to where to act.

title: Keeping current
heading: Reminders
text: Whoever something waits on is reminded two weeks before its date, and again the day after it passes. What stays late goes up. What has a date Who is told If it stays late An assessment about to expire Whoever is accountable for the application The unit's steward after a week, its leader after three A record due to be confirmed Whoever is accountable for the application The same A decision's target date Whoever is accountable for the application The same A decision's review date Whoever decided, or the unit's leaders if they have gone It stays with them A task Whoever the task is for The unit's steward, then its leader, where the task is about an application What a campaign asks Whoever was a

title: Keeping current
heading: By email, if you wish
text: Where email is set up, choose under Your account to have each notice as it happens, one summary a day, or none. Everything is always under the bell as well. Without email, nothing is sent and nothing is lost: see Configuration .

title: Keeping current
heading: Confirm the record
text: Every so often, the people who keep an application say that its record is right: its details, the people named on it, its components and what they are built on, what it sends and receives, where it runs, and what it costs. If something is wrong, put it right first, then confirm. Below an application's scores, a line says when its record was last confirmed, by whom, and when it is next due. Choose Confirm the record , add a note if you wish, and confirm. Tier Confirmed every 1 and 2 6 months 3, 4, and 5 12 months The people named on an application, its unit's stewards, and managers may confirm it. A record past its date is stale , and says so where everyone can see it: the line below its scor

title: Keeping current
heading: Campaigns
text: A campaign asks the people who answer for the applications in a unit to confirm their records, or to assess their applications, by a date. Managers and stewards run them over the units they hold their role for: under Portfolio → Campaigns , choose Start a campaign . Choose what to ask, the unit (everything beneath it is included), and, if you wish, only certain tiers or stages, a date, and a note. Before you start it, it says how many people it would ask about how many applications, and names any application with nobody to ask. Each application goes to whoever is accountable for it, or to a steward of its unit if they have gone. Each person is told once, with a count, and finds what is asked

title: Keeping current
heading: Tasks
text: Some things need someone to act because of what has happened, not because of a date anyone set. Each hour AppWren looks, and raises a task for the person who must act, with a date and the reason, and tells them. What happens Raised For Settled when A contract's notice date is near 60 days before it The contract's owner The term changes (it was renewed) or it ends A release in use nears its end of support 180 days before, for each application on it Whoever answers for the application Nothing of it runs on that release any more A grant nears its end 180 days before, for each application it pays for Whoever answers for the application A decision on the application is recorded An accountable own

title: Keeping current
heading: When someone leaves
text: Disabling an account does not move anything by itself: each application they were accountable for shows that nobody is, and a steward is given a task to name someone. Every person has a page of what they hold : the records they are named on and in what role, the contracts and interfaces they own, their open tasks, and what campaigns still ask of them. Open it from Admin → People , or from a notice. An administrator or a manager can Pass it all on to one person in one step; that person is told. Assessments and decisions are not passed on: each stays the statement of whoever made it.

title: Keeping current
heading: Find anything
text: Press ⌘K or Ctrl K , or / , and type: the command palette finds pages, actions, and records. Search everything lists every kind of record that matches, the best answer first, by name, reference, summary, or what something is called in another system. You find only what you may open.

title: Keeping current
heading: Saved views
text: Filter any list as you want it, then save it under a name from its Views button, to come back to it. Stewards, architects, and managers may share a view with everyone. A view keeps the question, never the answer: whoever opens it sees only what they may.

title: Keeping current
heading: Likely duplicates
text: While an application is added or renamed, AppWren shows any already on record whose name or alias is close to the new name, or that are the same product from the same vendor. If it is the same application, add to that record instead.

title: Keeping current
heading: Contest a score
text: If a factor of an application's scores is wrong, say so. On its Scores part, choose Contest a factor : which factor, what it should be, why, and a link to the evidence. Whoever keeps the application may. The portfolio team (a manager or an architect over its unit) sees it on Home and answers: they accept it, saying what will be changed, or they answer it, saying why not. You are told either way, and both stay on the record and in its history. A contest does not move a score. Scores come from the record and the assessment, so a contest that is right is put right there.

title: Keeping current
heading: Next
text: For who may do each of these, read Roles and scope . To change the periods, the penalty, or how far ahead tasks are raised, read Shape it in the app .

title: Planning change
heading: Planning change
text: Planning change This guide is for the people who decide what happens to applications, and for those who carry it out. It covers portfolio reviews, initiatives and the roadmap, requests for something new, stage gates, and retiring an application. A decision says what to do with an application ( Decisions ). This part of AppWren carries it through: the portfolio is reviewed with an agenda drawn from what needs deciding, what is decided becomes an initiative with dates, a request for something new is checked against what is there before anything is bought, an application cannot move on without what its next stage requires, and a retirement is a plan that ends with its savings on record.

title: Planning change
heading: Portfolio reviews
text: A review is a meeting about a unit's applications, and the record of what it decided. Under Portfolio → Reviews , a manager, or a leader of the unit, plans one: its name, the unit (with everything beneath it), the date, a chair, and, if wished, only certain tiers. Draw the agenda adds the applications in its scope that need deciding: Why it is on the agenda What that means The decision on record differs from today's recommendation Its decision and its scores no longer agree ( Mismatches ) Its decision is due for review Its decision's review date falls on or before the review No decision is on record It is in service and nobody has said what to do with it Added by hand Someone put it there, w

title: Planning change
heading: Initiatives and the roadmap
text: An initiative is a planned change: a modernization, a migration, a consolidation, a replacement, a retirement, or another. It is a record of its own ( INI-0001 ), with a unit, an owner, a stage (proposed, approved, under way, done, cancelled), dates, and a budget, and it names the applications it changes and what it does to each: changes it , retires it , or moves work onto it . Each is shown with the decision on record for it. An application's page lists the initiatives that change it. A decision to modernize, replace, consolidate, or retire offers Start an initiative on the application's Decisions part, with the application (and, for a consolidation, the one its users move to) already name

title: Planning change
heading: Requests for something new
text: Anyone may ask for something new under Portfolio → Requests : the need, the capability it serves, how many people would use it, and when it is needed. The request lists every application that already serves that capability, and any whose name is close to its own, so a duplicate is seen before it is bought. A steward of the unit, an architect, or a manager weighs the ways to meet it : build it, buy it, partner for it, or reuse an application on record, each with what it would cost a year and how well it fits, 1 to 5. Then they end it, once, with a reason: Approve : an application in the proposed stage is added, named for the request, serving its capability, in its unit. Nothing is built or bo

title: Planning change
heading: Stage gates
text: Each lifecycle stage requires some of the record ( What each stage requires ). An application cannot move to a later stage without what that stage, and those before it, require. The editor, the API, an import, and a catalog file are all refused, and say what is missing: Before it moves to Active, record sign-in, monitoring, backup, a current assessment. Moving back needs nothing. Neither does retiring: what is retired is not kept up, so a retirement is never stopped for want of a full record. The gates are on by default, and the portfolio team can switch them off on Admin → Program → Decisions ; a record then still shows what it lacks, but may move anyway.

title: Planning change
heading: Retiring an application
text: On an application's Retirement part, whoever keeps it starts a retirement plan with the date it is to be retired by; its planned retirement on the record moves to the same date. The plan is a checklist: Step What to note Its users told How, and when Its data archived, and where Where it is kept now, and for how long Its interfaces removed The part counts the interfaces on record Its licenses and contracts ended What was not renewed Access to it removed Accounts and groups taken away Its infrastructure torn down What was switched off or recycled Each step is marked done by a named person on a date, with a note, and can be undone until the plan is complete. When every step is done, Complete th

title: Insight
heading: Insight
text: Insight This guide is for the portfolio team and for leadership: those who ask how the portfolio is moving, where its cost and use are concentrated, and what happened over a quarter. It covers trends between snapshots, an application's scores over time, shares of the portfolio, leadership reports, the record as it stood on a past day, scenarios, and the optional assistant. Everything here is read from what AppWren already keeps. A portfolio snapshot keeps every scored application's scores as they were ( Portfolio snapshots ); a decision keeps the scores it was made on; and a leadership report, once made, keeps every figure in it. None of it is worked out again later from the records as they

title: Insight
heading: Trends
text: Reports → Trends puts two portfolio snapshots side by side, or one snapshot and today. For each it shows how many applications were scored, how many by recommendation, how many with low confidence, and the average of each score. Between them it lists: What moved What it means Recommendation changed Today's recommendation, or the later snapshot's, differs from the earlier one's Scores moved A score rose or fell by half a point or more Flags raised or cleared A flag came or went Added or gone Scored in one and not the other Decided between them Every decision recorded after the earlier snapshot was taken, up to the later one Each person sees what they may see: an application they cannot open i

title: Insight
heading: Shares of the portfolio
text: Reports → Shares of the portfolio names the applications at one end of the portfolio in service: Share Ranked by The costliest tenth Annual cost The dearest tenth per user Annual cost for each person who uses it The least used fifth Its count of users The oldest fifth Years since it went live Each share is worked out from the applications that have the figure it ranks by, and says how many do not. A share says where an application stands against the rest, not whether it costs too much or is used too little: that is for the scores and their defined bands ( The scores ), and a share never feeds a score. Cost is left out for anyone who may not see it.

title: Insight
heading: Leadership reports
text: A leadership report says, for a period, where the portfolio stood and what happened in it. A manager makes one under Reports → Leadership reports , with a title and a period that has ended, often the last quarter (which is suggested). It holds: Where the portfolio stood when it was made: the applications in service, what they cost together (for those who see every cost), how many by recommendation and by decision on record, what needs attention, the flags raised, and engineering maturity. How the scores moved : from the last portfolio snapshot before the period, or its first, to its last, with the change in each average score and how many applications changed recommendation, moved on a score

title: The program handbook
heading: The program handbook
text: The program handbook This guide is for the portfolio team: the people who run an application portfolio program with AppWren, from the first decisions to the yearly rhythm of reviews. The other guides say what each screen does. This one says what to do with them, in what order, and why. A portfolio program answers three questions about every application the organization runs, and keeps the answers true: what do we run, who answers for it, and what should we do with it? AppWren keeps the record, works out a recommendation from it, and holds the decision people take. The program is the people and the habits that keep all three current.

title: The program handbook
heading: 1. Decide before you start
text: A few decisions shape everything after them. Make them on paper first; each takes minutes in AppWren once made. Decision Why it matters Where it lives What counts as an application Everything is counted in applications. A definition people can apply the same way keeps the count meaningful Admin → Program, the definition; What counts as an application The units Every application belongs to one unit, which answers for it. Units are how work is shared out, how scope is set, and how leaders see their part Admin → Units Who decides A decision is taken by a manager, or a leader over the application's unit, and never by the person accountable for it. Decide who those people are Admin → People, role

title: The program handbook
heading: 2. The roles, as a program uses them
text: Role In a running program Member Everyone. Reads the catalog and keeps the applications they are named on Accountable owner Not a role but a name on each application: the one person who answers for it. Confirms its record and answers its assessment. Every application has exactly one Steward Keeps a unit's applications complete, chases what is missing, and runs campaigns for the unit Leader Sees a unit and everything beneath it, decides for it, and runs its portfolio reviews Architect Keeps the shared records (capabilities, technologies, vendors) and weighs scenarios Manager Runs the portfolio: decides anywhere, shapes the program, makes leadership reports Auditor Reads everything, including

title: The program handbook
heading: Weeks 1 to 2: the inventory
text: Bring in the applications you already know from a spreadsheet ( Import applications ). Do not chase completeness: name, unit, accountable owner, lifecycle stage, and sourcing are enough to begin. Portfolio → Applications and Reports → Data quality show what each record lacks. Then turn on what other systems already know ( Facts from other systems ): the identity provider lists applications people sign in to that are not on record ( Portfolio → Not on record ), and support dates arrive by themselves.

title: The program handbook
heading: Weeks 3 to 6: the first confirmation campaign
text: Start a campaign for one unit, asking each owner to confirm their records by a date ( Portfolio → Campaigns ). Owners are reminded, stewards and leaders are told what stays late, and the campaign closes each item by itself. A first campaign with one willing unit teaches more than any amount of planning; widen it once it works.

title: The program handbook
heading: Weeks 6 to 10: assessment
text: Ask the owners of tier 1 and tier 2 applications to assess them: nine questions, each with five described levels. With an assessment, an application's scores and recommendation mean something. Reports → Dashboard shows what is recommended across the portfolio, and how confident each recommendation is.

title: The program handbook
heading: Weeks 10 to 13: the first review and the first decisions
text: Hold a portfolio review for one unit ( Portfolio → Reviews ), with an agenda drawn from what needs deciding: applications whose decision differs from the recommendation, decisions due again, and those with none. Decide in the room. Each decision says what to do (invest, maintain, tolerate, modernize, replace, consolidate, retire, incubate, or assess further), why, by when, and when to look again. At the end of the quarter, make the first leadership report ( Reports → Leadership reports ). It is kept as it was made, so next quarter's can be set beside it.

title: The program handbook
heading: 4. The yearly rhythm
text: Once running, the program keeps a rhythm. Most of it AppWren runs by itself; people do the deciding. When What Who Where Continuously Values from other systems arrive; tasks are raised when a contract's notice date nears, a release in use nears its end of support, a grant ends, or an owner leaves AppWren Tasks, Home Continuously Each owner confirms their records on the cadence their tier sets (by default every six months for tiers 1 and 2, every year for the rest), and renews assessments as they expire (every year for tiers 1 and 2, every eighteen months to two years for the rest) Owners Home Every month A portfolio snapshot keeps every application's scores AppWren Reports → Trends Every qua

title: The program handbook
heading: Running a quarterly review well
text: Draw the agenda a week before and send it to the people who own what is on it. A review of twenty applications is plenty for an hour. Start with mismatches : a decision that no longer agrees with the recommendation is either a decision to revisit or a record to correct. Both are worth the time. Decide or defer, with a date. A decision to tolerate an application for a year is a decision. Leaving it undecided is not. Close the review when it ends. It becomes a record of what was decided, and nothing in it changes after.

title: The program handbook
heading: From decision to done
text: A decision to modernize, replace, consolidate, or retire offers Start an initiative , which puts the change on the roadmap with an owner, dates, and a budget. A request for something new is checked against what already serves the need before anything is bought. A retirement is a plan with a checklist that ends with the application retired and its savings on record. See Planning change .

title: The program handbook
heading: Before committing to a large change
text: Build a scenario first ( Portfolio → Scenarios ): name the applications that would be retired, consolidated, or replaced, and AppWren works out what it would save, whom it would affect, which interfaces would stop, and which capabilities would be left with nothing. Nothing changes until it becomes an initiative. See Insight .

title: The program handbook
heading: 5. Measures worth watching
text: Measure Read it from What good looks like Records confirmed on time Reports → Data quality Rising each quarter, then steady above nine in ten Applications with an accountable owner Reports → Data quality Every one. An application nobody answers for is the first thing to fix Recommendations made with low confidence Reports → Dashboard Falling, as assessments and facts from other systems fill in Decisions that differ from the recommendation Reports → Dashboard, Mismatches Few, and each with a reason someone would stand behind Applications past end of support Reports → Dashboard Falling, each with a decision and a date Savings from retirements Reports → Retirements Recorded for every retirement

title: The program handbook
heading: 6. What goes wrong, and what to do
text: Sign Likely cause What to do Owners ignore reminders Too many at once, or the first contact was a demand Start with one unit, explain why, and have the leader ask, not the portfolio team Scores nobody believes Thin records and old assessments Look at the confidence first. Fill in the record and reassess before arguing with the score. Owners can contest a score with evidence Reviews run long Agendas too big, or decisions reopened every time Smaller agendas, decisions with review dates a year out, and mismatches first The inventory grows faster than it is kept Everything counted as an application Revisit the definition: a server, a report, or a module is a component of something, not an applic
