title: Facts from other systems
heading: Facts from other systems
text: Facts from other systems This guide is for administrators who connect AppWren to the tools the organization already runs, and for everyone who reads what those tools supply. It covers connectors, values from other systems and overriding them, applications found that are not on record, push sources, catalog files, engineering maturity, and how all of this joins the scores.

title: Facts from other systems
heading: Nothing is connected until you connect it
text: A new installation makes no connection to anything. Each source is switched on separately, by an administrator, for one named source: A connector reads a source on a schedule: support dates, what the repositories know, who signs in. A push source is one of your own tools posting facts to AppWren with a key you issue. A catalog file is kept beside the code and imported by whoever keeps the application. Whatever arrives is marked with where it came from, recorded in the history like any other change, and never wins over a person: anyone who keeps the record can override it, with a reason.

title: Facts from other systems
heading: Connectors
text: Admin → Connectors lists the connectors set up, their recent runs, and the kinds of source AppWren can read. Choose Add beside a kind, name it, and give what is not secret (an address, an organization, a tenant). It is added switched off. Choose Check to see that it reaches its source, then Switch on . A credential never goes into AppWren. A connector that needs one names the environment variable that holds it, such as APPWREN_GITHUB_TOKEN ; the server reads it when the connector runs. The page shows only whether it is set. Give each credential the least access it needs, and only read access. Kind What it reads Credential End-of-life data Support dates for technology releases, from the publi

title: Facts from other systems
heading: End-of-life data
text: Give each technology its key in the dataset (on its record, End-of-life key : python , nodejs , postgresql ). Each run follows the same rules as support dates from a file : releases are added and dates updated, nothing is removed, and a date the dataset does not give is left as it is. A key the dataset does not know is listed as not matched.

title: Facts from other systems
heading: Source code hosting
text: Give the host ( https://github.com , or your GitHub Enterprise server) and the organization, as it appears in repository addresses. A component is read when its Repository is in that organization on that host. A repository the token cannot read is listed as not matched, and nothing else about it changes. Where the host will not say whether a repository has dependency alerts, its alerts are not known, which is not the same as none. An application whose every repository was read gets its maintainers from the people who changed them over 90 days. From only some of them the count would be too low, so then its own number stands.

title: Facts from other systems
heading: The identity provider
text: Give the tenant (its ID or domain) and the client ID of the registration AppWren reads with. Each application registered there is matched to a record: by its identifier at the provider, kept on the record as its Sign-in registration , or else by its name or one of its aliases. A matched application's users become the people who signed in to it over the last 30 days. One that matches nothing is listed under Not on record .

title: Facts from other systems
heading: A run
text: Each connector that is on runs daily, or as often as you set, on the scheduled work ; Run now runs it at once. A run reads everything first, under a time limit and a size limit on each answer, and only then writes, in one transaction. A run that fails changes nothing , and says why on the page. Every run is listed with what it read, what changed, what stayed the same, what a person's override kept, and what it could not match.

title: Facts from other systems
heading: Values from other systems
text: A value a source supplies is written to the record's own field, so every list, filter, export, and score reads one place. It is kept with its source and the time it was read. On the record, From other systems lists each one; a technology's releases table marks the dates that came from a source. Someone who keeps the record can Override a value, saying why the source is wrong. The override wins until it is removed with Use the source's value ; meanwhile the source's later readings wait beside it, and are shown. Changing such a field by hand on the record counts as an override too. Both are in the history, with who and why.

title: Facts from other systems
heading: Not on record
text: Portfolio → Not on record lists the applications registered with the identity provider that match no record, for stewards, architects, and managers. Each is listed once. Add makes an application record named for it, in a unit you choose, with the provider's identifier kept on it. The next run matches it and gives it its users. Dismiss says why it is not kept on record, such as a test registration. A dismissed one can be listed again. One that someone records by hand is matched by the next run and leaves the list; one the provider no longer lists, that nobody decided about, goes. A connector never makes a record by itself.

title: Facts from other systems
heading: Push sources
text: For a tool AppWren has no connector for, such as the service desk or monitoring, an administrator issues a push key under Admin → Connectors → Push keys . The key is shown once and kept only as a hash; if it is lost, revoke it and issue another. The tool posts facts with it: curl -X POST https://appwren.example.org/api/v1/facts \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $APPWREN_PUSH_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"facts": [ {"record": "APP-0042", "field": "incidents_90d", "value": 3, "observed_at": "2026-11-20T09:00:00Z"}, {"record": "APP-0042", "field": "tickets_90d", "value": 27} ]}' Each fact names a record by its reference, a field, a value, and optionally when it was observed (with i

title: Facts from other systems
heading: Catalog files
text: An application and its components can be described in a catalog-info.yaml kept beside their code. On an application's Components part, Export a catalog file writes one; Import one reads one back, showing first what would change. The file holds documents with kind , metadata , and spec . A System describes the application: its description , tags , lifecycle ( production , experimental , deprecated ), and links to its documentation and home page. Each Component or Resource describes one of its parts: its type ( service , website , library , database , and so on), its description, and its repository, from a github.com/project-slug annotation or a link of type source . A part is matched by the r

A check about code does not apply to a part that is not code, such as a database; code with no repository recorded cannot pass it. An application is at the level of its least mature com

Elsewhere it does not apply, which is not the same as unknown: it neither lowers confidence nor moves the score, so an application with no source scores exactly as befo

title: Running the program
heading: Running the program
text: Running the program This guide is for the portfolio team and for administrators. It covers who may do what, who sees what, the program and how to shape it, upgrading, the dashboard and data quality, portfolio snapshots, scheduled work and email, the history, appearance, and backing up. How the portfolio keeps itself current (reminders, confirmations, campaigns, and tasks) is in Keeping current .

title: Running the program
heading: Two kinds of authority
text: AppWren keeps judgment and administration apart. Managers run the portfolio. They keep any application, record decisions, take snapshots, and shape the program: the vocabularies, the fields, the questions, and the scoring model. Administrators run the installation: accounts, units, sign-in, and appearance. Administration does not by itself let anyone keep applications or record decisions. An administrator who also does that work holds a second role, and the history shows which they acted under.

title: Running the program
heading: Roles and scope
text: Everyone who can sign in is a member . The other six roles are given under Admin → People , or from the identity provider (see Single sign-on ). Role Scope May Member Their own applications Read the catalog, scores, recommendations, and decisions; keep, assess, and confirm the applications they are named on, and contest their scores Steward A unit and everything beneath it Add, edit, import, assess, and confirm its applications, and hand on who is accountable; record their interfaces, deployments, and cost lines; add contracts; run campaigns over it Leader A unit and everything beneath it See it, read its sensitive fields, cost lines, and contracts, and record decisions for its applications

title: Running the program
heading: Who sees what
text: The catalog is open. Every application, component, interface, deployment, capability, technology, hosting platform, funding source, and vendor is visible to everyone signed in, with each application's scores, recommendation, and decision. A portfolio is useful in proportion to how many people can find what already exists: a researcher looking for an approved tool, an engineer checking who else runs a database, a team about to buy what another department already has. Two things narrow that. Sensitive fields. By default annual cost, the sign-in method, backup, and the last restore test are sensitive. They are visible to the people named on the application, to stewards, leaders, and architects

title: Running the program
heading: Shape the program
text: The program is everything the portfolio team configures, kept in the database rather than in a file on the server: Part What it holds Vocabularies Lifecycle stages, sourcing, purpose, pace, domains, tiers, hosting, sign-in methods, monitoring, backup, funding, data classes and their sensitivity, kinds of component, vendor, technology, platform, and unit, the radar's rings, the roles people hold on an application, link kinds, interface methods and frequencies, environments, cost categories, the states of a data agreement, other systems, and the dispositions Fields The organization's own fields, each in a section of the application's form What each stage requires The fields and records an appl

title: Running the program
heading: Shape it in the app
text: Admin → Program is for managers of the whole organization and for administrators. Every change is checked by the same rules a pack is, and kept in the history. Lists. Rename a value, describe it, put the values in another order, add one, or retire one. A value in use is retired rather than removed: records keep it, and it is no longer offered. The lists AppWren's own rules read by key, such as the lifecycle stages, the tiers, sourcing, and the dispositions, can be renamed, described, and reordered, but not added to or retired. Fields. Add a field of your own to the application's form, in the section it belongs to, or change its label, help, section, and choices; say which fields are sensitiv

title: Running the program
heading: Or change it with a pack
text: Whoever runs the server can change the whole program as a file: export it, edit it, check it, and load it. uv run appwren program export -o program.json # edit program.json uv run appwren program import program.json --dry-run uv run appwren program import program.json The whole pack is checked before anything is loaded, and nothing is loaded unless all of it can be: every vocabulary a field names, every fact a rule reads, every weight in a profile. --dry-run says what would change and changes nothing. A vocabulary value that is in use is retired rather than removed: records keep it, and it is no longer offered. Capabilities are only ever added. Rename or retire one in the app. Loading the sa

title: Running the program
heading: Links to other systems
text: An application can carry its identifier in another system: a configuration item, a ticket queue, a repository. To have each shown as a link, give the system an address pattern in the external_systems vocabulary of the pack, with {id} where the identifier goes: {"key": "repository", "label": "Repository", "url": "https://code.example.org/{id}"} A pattern must begin https:// . A pack with any other pattern is refused. How a record stands elsewhere An application's record in another system of record (an AI-use review, a risk register entry, a security assessment) has a standing there: approved, open, closed. Where that system answers in JSON, give it a standing_url , and AppWren reads each link

title: Running the program
heading: Versions
text: The question bank and the scoring model are versioned . A version in use is never changed: publishing in the app, or loading a pack that changes either, makes a new version, and the old one stays, marked superseded. Every assessment names the version of the questions it answered, and every snapshot names the version of the model it used, so a decision made last year still shows exactly what its maker saw. Changing the scoring model changes every application's scores at once, the next time they are read. The preview in the app says which. Take a portfolio snapshot first if you want a record of the portfolio as it was.

title: Running the program
heading: What an upgrade does to the program
text: uv run appwren db upgrade adds whatever is new in the default program and never overwrites what you have shaped. New vocabularies arrive with their defaults. A vocabulary you have changed is left as you have it. The scoring model. Version 0.2.0 has a new default model: cost and burden is now annual cost 30, cost per user 15, license use 10, support effort 25, and change effort 20, and there are two new flags. If you are still running the previous default unchanged, the upgrade publishes the new one as a new version, and scores for cost and burden move. If you have shaped your model, it is kept as it is. To take the new factors, export the default from a fresh installation or copy them from t

title: Running the program
heading: Read the dashboard
text: Reports → Dashboard shows the whole portfolio, or one unit and everything beneath it, or one domain. The headline: applications in service, how many have a decision, mismatches between decision and recommendation, reviews that are due, low confidence, and what runs on technology past or near its end of support. Recommendations and decisions: how many of each disposition, side by side, and how many have no decision yet. Lifecycle and sourcing: where the portfolio is in its life, and where its software comes from. Flags: how many applications carry each. Confidence: how many applications are known well enough to judge, in four bands. What it costs a year, and what pays for it: by kind of cost

title: Running the program
heading: Home
text: Home is each person's page of what is waiting on them: applications they are named on that have not been assessed, whose assessment has expired, or whose record is due to be confirmed; their tasks; what a campaign asks of them; flags on their applications; and what their records lack. A steward or manager also sees the applications in scope that nobody is accountable for; a leader or manager, the applications in their units waiting on a decision; a manager or architect, contests waiting for an answer. See Keeping current .

title: Running the program
heading: Data quality
text: Reports → Data quality shows, unit by unit, how complete the records are: applications with nobody accountable, no capability, no assessment, an expired assessment, low confidence, a record not confirmed in time, or something missing that their stage requires. Each figure opens its list. Choose a unit to see only it and the units beneath it. A portfolio's recommendations are only as good as its records, and this page is how the work of keeping them is shared out: give each steward the row for their unit.

title: Running the program
heading: Portfolio snapshots
text: A portfolio snapshot keeps every application's scores, recommendation, and working as they were on a day, under a name such as 2026 Q4 . Managers take them from Portfolio → Decisions → Snapshots with Take a snapshot , typically before each portfolio review and before changing the scoring model. The scheduler also takes one each month by itself, named for the month, so there is always a record of how the portfolio stood. A snapshot reopens unchanged after the applications or the program have changed. Its digest is recorded in the history, so a snapshot altered afterwards is detectable. Every decision also keeps a snapshot of the one application it was made about.

title: Running the program
heading: Scheduled work and email
text: AppWren does some work by itself, so that nobody has to remember to. Admin → Scheduled work shows each job, when it last ran and what it did, and can run it now or pause it. Job How often What it does Triggers Every hour Raises a task when a contract's notice date is near, a release nears its end of support, a grant nears its end, or an owner leaves; closes tasks whose cause is settled Reminders Every hour Reminds people of what is nearly due or late, and tells stewards and leaders what stays late; closes campaign items whose thing has been done Email Every minute Sends notices and daily summaries, where email is set up Standings elsewhere Every six hours Reads how each linked record stands

title: Running the program
heading: The history
text: Every change to every record is written to an append-only history in the same transaction as the change: who, when, and each value before and after. Each event is hashed together with the one before it, and the database itself refuses updates and deletes on the history. Each record's History part shows its own events in plain words: what was changed, and what was added to it, such as an assessment, a decision, a cost line, or a capability it serves. Changes to a sensitive field, and to cost lines, are withheld from people who may not see them. Reports → History shows every change in one place, for managers, auditors, and administrators: narrowed to a person, a record, a kind of record, or a

title: Running the program
heading: Appearance
text: Admin → Appearance makes the product yours, with a live preview: the product's name and your organization's name; a logo for light and for dark mode, and a tab icon; the default palette (Wren, Slate, or Garnet) and an accent color, which is adjusted for dark mode and refused if text on it could not be read; how scores are colored: an ordinal ramp in one hue from pale to deep, which keeps scores apart from the colors of flags, or a signal ramp from red through amber to green; an accent for dark mode, if the one worked out from your accent is not your brand's; a message and a picture on the sign-in page, up to five links at the foot of the sidebar and the sign-in page (your policy, your help d

title: Running the program
heading: Back up and recover
text: Back up with uv run appwren backup , which writes the database and the data home's files to one file, on SQLite or PostgreSQL alike ( Back up and restore ). Notices, reminders sent, and the email outbox are in the database; nothing about them needs backing up apart. uv run appwren program export keeps a copy of the program you have shaped. If nobody can sign in, appwren users adds an administrator or resets a password from the server's own command line. Changes made there are recorded in the history as made at the command line.

title: Configuration
heading: Configuration
text: Configuration This guide is for whoever runs the server. It covers appwren.toml , environment overrides, the data home, scheduled work, email, single sign-on, PostgreSQL, upgrading, running behind a reverse proxy, and the guard on demo installations.

title: Configuration
heading: What is configured where
text: AppWren keeps two kinds of settings apart. Kind Where it lives Examples How the server runs appwren.toml and the environment Address, port, database, data home The program and the product's look The database, set in the app or by a program pack Vocabularies, fields, what each stage requires, the questions, the scoring model, name, logo, colors This guide is about the first. For the second, see Running the program .

title: Configuration
heading: Where the file is found
text: uv run appwren init writes a commented appwren.toml in the current directory. Every command looks for the file in this order: The --config FILE option (short form -c ), given before the command. The APPWREN_CONFIG environment variable. ./appwren.toml . uv run appwren --config /etc/appwren/appwren.toml doctor Relative paths in the file are resolved against the file's own directory, not the directory you run from. An installation therefore moves as a unit.

title: Configuration
heading: Every section and key
text: The file has seven sections. Only the first three matter for a new installation; [sso] , [mail] , [assistant] , and [branding] are optional. A section or key that AppWren does not know is an error, not something it ignores. Every problem in the file is reported together.

title: Configuration
heading: Secrets are refused in the file
text: appwren.toml is meant to be safe to read, copy, and keep under version control. AppWren refuses to start if the file holds a secret: a key that looks like a password, secret, token, or key, or a database address with a password in it. Put secrets in the environment instead. For the database, set the password in PGPASSWORD , or put the whole address, password and all, in APPWREN_DATABASE_URL . The mail server's password goes in the variable [mail] password_env names, and single sign-on's client secret in the one [sso] client_secret_env names.

title: Configuration
heading: The data home
text: The data home is created by init . With the default settings it is ./var . Path Holds The SQLite database When no database address is set brand/ Uploaded logos and the tab icon logs/ The server's log, rotated files/ Reserved for attachments, each stored once under the SHA-256 of its content. Nothing here is served directly exports/ Reserved for exports .appwren-home A marker that says this directory is a data home Back it up with appwren backup ( Back up and restore ), which takes the database and the files here together. Do not edit its contents by hand. It must be writable by the account that runs the server. Request bodies and tokens are never written to the log.

title: Configuration
heading: Scheduled work
text: The server runs AppWren's scheduled work by itself while it is up: it raises tasks, sends reminders and email, takes the monthly snapshot, and tidies up. Admin → Scheduled work shows how it is going; see Running the program . Each job is claimed by one process before it runs, so any number of workers or servers on one database run it once between them. If you would rather run it from a scheduled task (cron, a systemd timer, a Kubernetes CronJob), set scheduler = false and run every few minutes: uv run appwren jobs run uv run appwren jobs lists the jobs, when each last ran, and what it did; uv run appwren jobs run reminders runs one now. doctor warns when the scheduler is off and nothing has

title: Configuration
heading: With another provider
text: Register AppWren as a confidential web client with the redirect address above. Set issuer to the address whose /.well-known/openid-configuration the provider serves, and client_id to what it gave you. Have it put a person's groups or roles in a claim, and name that claim in roles_claim (many providers call it groups ). If the provider says email_verified is true for its addresses, leave trust_email as it is.

title: Configuration
heading: Who a person is
text: A person is known by the provider's own identifier for them, never by an address alone. The first time someone signs in: if an account here has the address the provider vouches for, the two are joined, and from then on the provider's identifier is what counts; otherwise an account is made for them, with the roles their mappings give, unless create_accounts is false . A disabled account cannot come in through the provider. Signing out of AppWren does not sign anyone out of the provider.

title: Configuration
heading: Passwords, once it is on
text: With local_sign_in = true , anyone who has a password may still use it. With false , only administrators may. There is no setting that removes the administrator's password, on purpose: it is the way in when the provider cannot be reached.

title: Configuration
heading: Try it on a laptop
text: scripts/dev_identity_provider.py is a stand-in provider for trying this out. It has a fixed list of people and no passwords, and its signing key is published in the file, so it proves nothing and listens only on the machine it runs on. uv run python scripts/dev_identity_provider.py Then set issuer = "http://127.0.0.1:8099" , client_id = "appwren-dev" , and trust_email = true under [sso] , and start AppWren with APPWREN_SSO_CLIENT_SECRET=dev-secret in its environment.

title: Configuration
heading: Use PostgreSQL
text: SQLite is the default and needs no setup. Use PostgreSQL when many people will use AppWren at once or you want more than one server process. The features and the data model are the same on both, and the test suite runs on both. Install the driver, which is optional: `` bash uv sync --extra postgres `` Create an empty database and a role that owns it, with your usual PostgreSQL tools. Set the address in appwren.toml , without the password: `` toml [database] url = "postgresql+psycopg://appwren@db.example.org:5432/appwren" `` Put the password in the environment, then set up and check: `` bash export PGPASSWORD=… uv run appwren init uv run appwren doctor `` An installation already running on SQ

title: Configuration
heading: Back up and restore
text: uv run appwren backup --out appwren-backup.tar.gz A backup is one gzipped file: every table, as lines of JSON, every file in the data home's brand/ and files/ , and a manifest that says which version and migration made it and how many rows each table held. It can be made while the server is running: the tables are read in one transaction, so they agree with each other. The file does not depend on the kind of database, so a backup of SQLite restores into PostgreSQL and the other way round. It holds everything, password hashes included, and is written readable by its owner only: keep it as carefully as the database. To restore, set up an installation whose database is empty (a new appwren.toml

title: Configuration
heading: Move to another database
text: export NEW_DATABASE_URL=postgresql+psycopg://appwren:…@db.example.org:5432/appwren uv run appwren db move --to-env NEW_DATABASE_URL db move makes a backup and restores it into the new database, which must be empty, then verifies the history there. The old database is left as it was. Point the configuration at the new one ( [database] url , or APPWREN_DATABASE_URL ) and start the server. --to takes the address itself; --to-env names an environment variable that holds it, which keeps a password off the command line and out of the shell's history.

title: Configuration
heading: How many server processes
text: One process serves a small team well, and is all SQLite should be given: SQLite allows one writer at a time, and serve warns when several workers share one SQLite file. With PostgreSQL, add processes when many people work at once: [server] workers = 4 Each process is a whole server. They share nothing but the database and the data home: Sign-in sessions are kept in the database, so a person stays signed in whichever process answers. Scheduled work is claimed in the database before it runs, so a job runs once however many processes there are. The history is appended under a lock on its last entry, so it stays a single line.

title: Configuration
heading: Run behind a reverse proxy
text: AppWren speaks plain HTTP and expects a reverse proxy to terminate TLS in front of it. Keep host = "127.0.0.1" when the proxy is on the same machine. Have the proxy send X-Forwarded-Proto: https . AppWren marks its session cookie Secure when the request arrived over HTTPS, by that header or directly. Forward the Host header unchanged. Requests that change anything are refused when their origin does not match the host, which is part of the protection against requests from other sites. Requests larger than 32 MB are refused. title: Configuration
heading: The demo and the network
text: A demo organization signs in anyone who asks as any of its sample people, with no password. So a demo's server listens only on the machine it runs on: serve refuses any other host, and the sample sign-in refuses requests from other machines. If you do want to show a demo to others on a network you trust: uv run appwren --config demo/appwren.toml serve --host 0.0.0.0 --demo-on-network Anyone who can reach it can then sign in as the demo's portfolio manager or administrator. Never do this with a database that holds anything real; a demo database holds nothing that is.

title: The API
heading: The API
text: API Everything the web app does, it does through a JSON API under /api/v1 . This guide covers how to sign in, how answers and errors are shaped, how lists page, and what routes there are. The exact shape of every request and answer is in the OpenAPI document: openapi.json in this directory, or /api/openapi.json on a running server. A program signs in as an account, with that account's password, and holds a session as a browser does. The one exception is posting facts: a tool holding a push key an administrator issued posts to POST /api/v1/facts with the key and no session, and can do nothing else with it (see Facts from other systems ). Until 1.0, routes may change between releases. Changes

title: The API
heading: Changing things
text: Every request that changes anything ( POST , PUT , PATCH , DELETE ) must carry the session's CSRF token in a header: curl -s -b cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'X-CSRF-Token: …' \ -d '{"name": "Freezer Watch", "sourcing": "built_here", "lifecycle": "active", "tier": "2", "org_unit_id": 4}' \ http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/applications Without it the answer is 403. If the request carries an Origin header, it must match the host, or the request is refused.

title: The API
heading: Sign in as another system
text: A script or another system signs in with an API token instead of a session. An administrator issues one under Admin → API tokens : for one role (any but administrator), for one unit and those beneath it if the role has a unit, for reading only unless they say otherwise, and until a day at most a year away. The token is shown once; only its SHA-256 is kept. Send it with each request: curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer awt_…' http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/applications A token sees and may do what its role may, and nothing more. A reading token is refused any change with 403. A change made with a token is recorded in the history against the token's name. A token needs no CSRF token, since no brow

title: The API
heading: A token of your own
text: Anyone may make a token of their own under Your account → Your API tokens . It acts as them, so it sees exactly what they see; it reads, and it proposes changes, and it changes nothing itself. A proposal is a suggestion on an application: a value for one field, with a note saying why. It waits on the application's page until someone who keeps the application accepts it, which is their own edit, checked by the usual rules and kept in the history under their name, or dismisses it. curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer awt_…' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"field": "users", "value": 95, "note": "The sign-in log says so"}' \ http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/applications/APP-0024/suggestions

heading: Let an AI assistant read AppWren

title: The API
heading: Editing a record someone else is editing
text: Records carry a version . Send the version you read with a PATCH , and if someone else has changed the record since, the answer is 409 and nothing is saved. Read it again and decide what to do.

title: The API
heading: Answers
text: Every successful answer has the same envelope: {"data": …, "meta": {…}} data is one object or a list. meta carries what is about the answer and not in it: paging for a list, or a count of what else changed. Times are UTC in ISO 8601. Dates with no time, such as a review date, are YYYY-MM-DD .

title: The API
heading: Errors
text: Errors are problem documents ( application/problem+json ): { "type": "about:blank", "title": "Unprocessable Entity", "status": 422, "detail": "The decision was not recorded.", "errors": [ {"location": ["rationale"], "message": "Say why. The next person to look at it will want to know."} ], "instance": "/api/v1/applications/APP-0042/decisions" } Status Meaning 400 The request could not be carried out as asked 401 Nobody is signed in, or the email address and password do not match 403 You are signed in but may not do this, or the CSRF token is missing. detail says which 404 No such thing, or none that you may see. title: Command reference
heading: Command reference
text: Command reference Every appwren command. This page is written from the program itself, so it always matches the version it ships with. Run commands with uv run appwren … from the project directory. Options that come before the command apply to all of them: appwren [-h] [--version] [-c FILE] [-v | -q] COMMAND ...

title: Command reference
heading: Commands
text: Command What it does appwren init Set up a new installation appwren serve Run the web server appwren db Look after the database schema appwren tools Let an AI assistant read AppWren and propose changes appwren backup Write the whole installation to one file appwren restore Load a backup into an empty installation appwren users Manage accounts from the command line appwren verify Check that the history has not been altered appwren demo Build a fictional organization to explore appwren program Move the program between installations appwren technologies Bring technology support dates in from a file appwren jobs See scheduled work, or run it now appwren mail Send waiting email, or test the mail

title: Command reference
heading: appwren init
text: Write a configuration file if there is none, create the data home, create or upgrade the database, create the organization's top unit if there are no units, and create the first administrator if there is none. Safe to run again. Option Meaning --force overwrite an existing configuration file --admin-email EMAIL create the first administrator with this address --admin-name NAME the first administrator's name --program STARTER begin from a starter program, such as starter-university (see: appwren program starters) --organization NAME the organization's name, as its top unit, if there are no units yet --first-unit NAME a first unit within the organization, such as the team starting with AppWren

title: Command reference
heading: appwren serve
text: Run AppWren's web server. It refuses to start on a database whose schema is behind; run appwren db upgrade first. Option Meaning --host address to listen on (default: from the configuration) --port PORT port to listen on (default: from the configuration) --workers WORKERS server processes (default: from the configuration) --reload restart when the code changes (development) --demo-on-network let a demo organization listen beyond this machine (anyone who reaches it can sign in as its sample people)

title: Command reference
heading: appwren db
text: Look after the database schema.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren db upgrade
text: Apply any migrations the database has not had. Export first: an upgrade cannot be undone except by restoring.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren db current
text: Show which migration the database is at, and which this version expects. Exits with 1 when they differ.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren db move
text: Copy every table into another database that has not been set up, such as from SQLite to PostgreSQL or back, by way of a backup. The history is verified in the new database. The old one is left as it was. Option Meaning --to URL the new database's address --to-env NAME the name of an environment variable holding the address, to keep a password off the command line

title: Command reference
heading: appwren tools
text: An optional tool server for AI assistants, speaking the Model Context Protocol. It is not needed to run AppWren.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren tools serve
text: Serve AppWren's tools to an AI assistant over standard input and output. An assistant's host program starts this command; it is not run by hand. It calls the AppWren at APPWREN_URL with the token in APPWREN_TOKEN, a token of the person's own, and so sees only what they may. It reads records and proposes changes. It cannot change, decide, or accept anything.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren backup
text: Write every table, every attachment and brand file, and a manifest to one gzipped tar. It can be made while the server is running. The file does not depend on the kind of database, so it restores into SQLite or PostgreSQL. It holds everything in the installation: keep it as carefully as the database itself. Option Meaning --out FILE where to write it (default: appwren-backup-DATE.tar.gz)

title: Command reference
heading: appwren restore
text: Load a backup into the configured database and data home. The database must hold no accounts and no history: nothing is ever overwritten. The history is verified once it is loaded. Option Meaning FILE the backup, a .tar.gz written by appwren backup

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users
text: Manage accounts from the command line: for setting up, and for getting back in when nobody can sign in. Everyday account management is in the app, under Admin. Changes made here are recorded in the history as made at the command line.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users add
text: Add an account. It asks for a password unless --password-stdin or --invite is given. Option Meaning EMAIL the email address the person signs in with --name the person's name --title their job title --role ROLE a role: admin, manager, architect, auditor, steward=unit:CODE, or leader=unit:CODE; manager and architect may also take unit:CODE (may be repeated) --unit CODE a unit they work in, by code (may be repeated) --password-stdin read the password from standard input instead of asking --invite add them without a password: they can be named on records now, and sign in once they are given a password or use single sign-on

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users list
text: List every account with its status and roles.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users disable
text: Stop an account signing in and end its sessions. Its records and history are kept. The last active administrator cannot be disabled. Option Meaning EMAIL the account's email address

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users enable
text: Let a disabled account sign in again. Option Meaning EMAIL the account's email address

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users reset-password
text: Give an account a new password and end its sessions. Option Meaning EMAIL the account's email address --password-stdin read the password from standard input instead of asking

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users roles
text: Show an account's roles, or with --set replace the roles granted in AppWren. Roles mapped from an identity provider are left alone. The last active administrator cannot lose that role. Option Meaning EMAIL the account's email address --set ROLE a role: admin, manager, architect, auditor, steward=unit:CODE, or leader=unit:CODE; manager and architect may also take unit:CODE (may be repeated); with none, removes every role

title: Command reference
heading: appwren verify
text: Recompute the hash chain over every event in the history and report the first one that does not hold. Exits with 1 if the history is broken.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren demo
text: Build the Bramblewood Institute for Health Research, a fictional organization with two years of history, in its own directory. Everything in it is made by the same code the app uses. Start it with the command it prints. Option Meaning PATH where to build it (default: ./demo) --seed SEED a different number gives a different Bramblewood --port PORT the port its server will use (default: 8020) --force rebuild a demo that is already there

title: Command reference
heading: appwren program
text: The program is everything a portfolio team configures: vocabularies, the organization's own fields, what each lifecycle stage requires, sensitive fields, the capability map, the questions, and the scoring model. It lives in the database and moves as one file.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren program export
text: Write the whole program as one JSON document, to a file or to standard output. Option Meaning --output , -o FILE write to this file

title: Command reference
heading: appwren program import
text: Load a program pack. The whole pack is checked first, and nothing is loaded unless all of it can be. A vocabulary value in use is retired rather than removed, and capabilities are only ever added. Option Meaning FILE the pack to load, or the key of a starter program --dry-run say what would change, and change nothing

title: Command reference
heading: appwren program starters
text: List the starter programs: the default program as a research institute, an academic medical center, a university, a nonprofit, or a company would first change it. Begin a new installation from one with init --program, or load one over a program with program import.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren technologies
text: Technologies and their releases are kept in the app. Their support dates can also be brought in from a file, so that nobody types them. AppWren does not fetch the file: you bring it.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren technologies import-eol
text: Read a JSON file of end-of-life data: one object whose keys are products and whose values are lists of releases, each with a cycle and any of releaseDate, eol, extendedSupport, and latest. A product is matched to the technology whose end-of-life key it is. Releases are added and dates updated; nothing is removed. Option Meaning FILE the file to read --dry-run say what would change, and change nothing

title: Command reference
heading: appwren jobs
text: Scheduled work sends reminders, and sends email where that is set up. The server does this by itself while it runs. These commands are for seeing how it is going, and for running it from a scheduled task where the server's own scheduler is turned off.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren jobs run
text: Run every job that is due. With a job's name, run that one now whether or not it is due. A job another process is running is left to it. Option Meaning JOB one job to run now

title: Command reference
heading: appwren mail
text: Email is optional. Where it is set up, the server sends it by itself while it runs. These commands are for testing the settings and for sending by hand.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren mail run
text: Queue notices and daily summaries, and send what is waiting. Exits with 1 if a message could not be sent.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren mail test
text: Send one message now to the account with this address, and say whether the mail server accepted it. Option Meaning EMAIL the account to send it to

title: Command reference
heading: appwren doctor
text: Check the configuration, the data home, the database and its schema, and the history. Exits with 1 if anything must be fixed. Option Meaning --production also check what matters once people depend on it: an https address, the database, administrators, sign-in, email, scheduled work, backups, and who can read the data home; a demo organization fails

What it found is fixed, each with a test: a new password now revokes the account's own tokens; the checkpoint and the assistant leave out fields the program marks sensitive; a proposed value has a size limit; an identifier cannot climb a standing address; and a token never administers.

An installation is backed up, restored, and moved between SQLite and PostgreSQL by command, and is measured at five thousand applications. It wears the organization's own colors, logo files, typefaces, and words; begins from a starter program shaped like the organization; lets other systems in with tokens limited to a role and tells them what happens with signed webhooks; and is deployed from recipes checked by doctor --production . title: Changelog
heading: Fixed
text: Pages that read every application failed on SQLite past about 32,000 components, from the database's limit on query parameters. The dashboard, data quality, overlap, the portfolio list, Home, and shares of the portfolio are two to twenty times faster on a large portfolio.

title: Changelog
text: Wave 6, Insight : the record read back as a whole, for leadership. Two portfolio snapshots side by side say what moved between them, and an application's scores are shown over time; shares of the portfolio name the costliest and least used applications without feeding any score; a leadership report for a period is worked out once and kept whole, with a digest that shows it is unchanged; the portfolio, and any application, can be seen as it stood at the end of a chosen day, from the history; and a scenario shows what a set of changes would save, whom it would affect, and what would stop, before anyone commits to it.

title: Changelog
heading: Added
text: Trends. Reports → Trends puts two portfolio snapshots side by side, or one and today: the figures each held, the applications whose recommendation changed, whose scores rose or fell by half a point or more, and whose flags came or went, applications added or gone, and the decisions recorded between them. An application's Scores part shows its scores over time. Shares of the portfolio. Reports → Shares of the portfolio lists the costliest tenth, the dearest tenth per user, the least used fifth, and the oldest fifth of the applications in service. A share never feeds a score. Leadership reports. A manager makes a report for a period under Reports → Leadership reports: where the portfolio stood

title: Changelog
heading: Changed
text: Three more rarely opened dialogs on a record's page (the people named on it, the capabilities it serves, and what it is called elsewhere) load when they are opened.

title: Changelog
text: Wave 5, Planning change : decisions become planned, tracked change. A portfolio review draws its agenda from what needs deciding and keeps what it decided; a decision to change something becomes an initiative with its applications and dates, on a roadmap; a request for something new is checked against what already serves the need before anything is bought; an application cannot move to a later stage without what that stage requires; and a retirement is a plan with a checklist that ends with the application retired and its savings on record. Upgrade with uv sync and uv run appwren db upgrade . Every row and file is kept, and no score moves. Stage gates are on after the upgrade: see Changed .

title: Changelog
heading: Added
text: Portfolio reviews. Under Portfolio → Reviews, a manager or a unit's leader plans a review of a unit and everything beneath it, narrowed by tier if wished, with a date and a chair. Drawing the agenda adds the applications that need deciding: those whose decision differs from today's recommendation, whose decision is due for review by then, or that have none; more can be added by hand. Each item shows what was recommended and decided before, and a decision recorded while the review is open is shown on its item and kept there when it closes. A closed review changes no more. heading: Changed
text: Home gives tasks, campaigns, and reviews icons of their own. Three rarely opened dialogs on a record's page (what a component is built on, a technology's releases, and what a contract covers) load when they are opened. Breaking: with the gates on by default, an import or an API call that moves an application to a later stage without what that stage requires is now refused. Switch the gates off to keep the old behaviour.

title: Changelog
text: Wave 4, Signals : the facts other tools already know arrive by themselves, marked with where they came from, and never over a person. Connectors, each switched on by an administrator for one named source, read support dates, what the repositories know, and who signs in; the organization's own tools post the rest with a key that can do nothing else; a catalog file kept beside the code describes an application and its components. Engineering maturity is measured from checks rather than claims, and what sources supply joins the scores only where they supply it. A new installation still makes no connection to anything. title: Changelog
heading: Added
text: Connectors. Admin → Connectors lists the tools AppWren can read facts from. Each connector is added switched off, for one named source; it only reads; its credential stays in an environment variable named on the connector and is never stored. It can be checked before it is switched on, runs daily on the scheduler or when asked, and every run is recorded: what it read, what it changed, what it could not match, and why it failed. A run reads everything first, under a time limit and a size limit, and writes only if all of that succeeded, so a failed run changes nothing. Values from other systems. heading: Changed
text: A scoring model's dimension adds up to 100 without its signals; a signal comes on top. The API fetches nothing an administrator has not switched on. A push key is the one credential besides a session, and it only posts facts.

title: Changelog
text: Wave 3, Keeping current : a portfolio that stays true without a central team chasing it. The app knows what falls due and says so, in the app and by email; owners confirm their records on a cadence, and a record nobody confirms lowers confidence where everyone can see it; campaigns ask the owners in a unit, by a date; departures, renewals, end of support, and grant ends raise tasks for whoever must act; anything on record can be found; and the program is shaped in the app, with a preview of what a change would do. Upgrade with uv sync and uv run appwren db upgrade . Every row and file is kept, and no record is stale on the day of the upgrade.

title: Changelog
heading: Changed
text: The default scoring model gains the cadence of wave 3: how often records are confirmed and what a stale one costs, when reminders go, and how far ahead tasks are raised. An upgrade brings it to a model that nobody has changed since 0.1.0 or 0.2.0; one the organization has shaped is left alone and uses the same values until it says otherwise.

title: Changelog
heading: Fixed
text: A bubble on the portfolio chart opened a page that was not there. Links inside a drawing were followed by the wrong address. Clicking a bubble now opens its application, and hovering one shows which application it is and where it stands. Present since 0.1.0. The demo's research software engineer was named on no application, though the guides sent people to see the applications they keep. They now keep the two pieces of research software in the demo's storylines.

title: Changelog
text: Wave 2, The landscape : each application in its surroundings. What it sends and receives and what data passes, what depends on it and what breaks if it goes, where it runs, what it costs and what pays, the contracts behind it, what else does the same job, and what it is built on that is falling out of support. Upgrade with uv sync and uv run appwren db upgrade . Every row and file is kept.

heading: Added
text: Interfaces. Data passing from one application to another is a record of its own, with a reference ( INT-0007 ), a method, how often, the classes of data it carries, and an owner. title: Changelog
heading: Changed
text: An application that receives data through an interface now counts among the dependents of the application that sends it, so recording interfaces can raise a source's business value. The default scoring model has a new version. Cost and burden is now annual cost 30, cost per user 15, license use 10, support effort 25, and change effort 20, so scores for cost and burden move. An installation still running the previous default gets the new one on upgrade; one that has shaped its model keeps it, and can take the new factors from the default program when it chooses. A record's history names the vendor, application, or person a change refers to, where it showed a number.

title: Changelog
heading: Fixed
text: A record's history told an assessment, a decision, a capability served, and a unit that uses an application each as "Added this application". Each is now told for what it is, and the copy of a decision onto its application is no longer told as a second change.

title: Changelog
text: Wave 1, The portfolio : install, sign in, and keep one record of every application, with what it is built on and what it does for the organization; assess it, read four scores with their working, see the recommendation and its rule, and record what people decided.

title: Changelog
heading: Added
text: Foundation. appwren init , serve , db upgrade , db current , verify , and doctor . Deployment settings in appwren.toml with environment overrides; secrets are refused in the file. SQLite by default and PostgreSQL by address, on one model and one set of migrations. Every change is written to an append-only, hash-chained history in the same transaction, and appwren verify finds the first event that has been altered. Accounts and roles. Local accounts with scrypt-hashed passwords, server-side sessions, CSRF protection, and throttled sign-in. Seven roles: admin, manager, architect, auditor, leader, steward, and member, some limited to a unit and everything beneath it. Every API route is checked
